"He leaned back the whole time," Aparna said, dropping her bag on the sofa. "Feet on the chair, hands behind his head. Is my new boss bored with me?"

"Or he is comfortable," Akash said. "What was he like when you spoke?"

"He asked good questions. And he remembered my old project."

"So maybe leaning back is just how he is. My old boss stood right over people's desks and it was only because his own chair was broken."

"Ha. But last office, the manager sat upright, very formal."

"Different offices, different habits."

"I will watch what he does over a few weeks instead of guessing."

qa.q: What did Aparna's new boss do with his feet?
qa.a: He had his feet on the chair.

qa.q: What was Aparna worried about, and how did Akash's questions change her view?
qa.a: She worried her boss was bored with her, but Akash pointed out he asked good questions and remembered her project. That evidence suggests leaning back may just be his style.

qa.q: What is a sensible way for Aparna to judge her boss's attitude?
qa.a: She can watch how he behaves over a few weeks instead of guessing from posture alone.

qa.q: How might the boss see his own posture?
qa.a: He may simply feel comfortable and not realise it looks casual or bored to a new employee.

grounding: Dialogue about a young professional meeting a boss who leans back, where posture signals status differently across offices and behaviour over time tells more.

passage: My first job, in Nairobi, was under a manager who sat tall and still, and I thought she was cold. My second, in Chennai, had a boss who leaned back and talked to me with his hands behind his head, and I first felt disrespected. I am Suraj, and I have spent a while working out what posture actually means. Nothing certain, I found. The tall manager turned out to be shy and gave generous feedback. The leaning boss was laid-back but sharp, and fully supportive when I made mistakes. When a third boss stood close beside my desk, I paused before deciding it was pushy. Naveen, my mentor, told me, "Watch what people do over time." That advice saved me from a lot of wrong guesses.

qa.q: Where was Suraj's first job?
qa.a: His first job was in Nairobi.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel about each boss at first, and what was the truth?
qa.a: He felt the tall manager was cold and the leaning boss was disrespectful. In time the manager turned out to be shy and generous, and the leaning boss was laid-back and supportive.

qa.q: What advice helped Suraj avoid wrong guesses?
qa.a: His mentor Naveen said to watch what people do over time.

qa.q: How might the leaning boss have seen his own posture?
qa.a: He probably saw it as relaxed and comfortable, not as a sign of status or disrespect.

grounding: First-person account of a young professional whose bosses lean back, sit tall or stand close, learning that posture alone is a poor guide.

passage:
Mentoring note, week 6. Written by Elizabeth, graduate programme mentor, Leeds office.
Baljeet told me today that she had been dreading her one-to-ones with Graham, the director. "He leans right back with his hands behind his head while I talk," she said. "At home, that would mean he doesn't care." In her last job in Chandigarh, she said, senior people sat very upright and juniors stood.
I have watched Graham with her for six weeks. The lean-back is how he sits with everyone, including the chief executive. More telling: he has read every draft she has sent and forwarded her analysis to the board with her name on it.
I shared this with Baljeet and suggested she judge him by what he does over time rather than how he sits. She laughed and said, "So the lean-back isn't an insult?"
Next step: we will review in a month how the one-to-ones feel.

qa.q: Where was Baljeet's last job?
qa.a: In Chandigarh.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling about the one-to-ones with Graham?
qa.a: She felt dread and some hurt, reading his lean-back as not caring, based on how seniors sat in her last job.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth suggest, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: To judge Graham by what he does over time rather than how he sits, since reading her drafts and crediting her to the board show real interest.

qa.q: How does Graham's posture look from Elizabeth's six weeks of watching?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees the lean-back as simply his habit with everyone, even the chief executive, not a sign of disrespect toward Baljeet.

grounding: A mentor notes a young professional misreading a boss's leaning-back posture across office cultures and learning to judge by behaviour over time.

passage:
Thursday, late
New boss, day four. Sunaina ma'am does this thing: when she comes to your desk she stands right beside the chair, close enough that I can smell her coffee, and looks down at the screen. In meetings she sits bolt upright at the head of the table and never leans back. This morning my first thought was: she's checking on me, she doesn't trust me. My shoulders were up round my ears till lunch.
But then at six, when my report crashed, she pulled a chair over, sat next to me at the same height, and spent forty minutes fixing the formulas with me. She even laughed at my terrible file names.
So what does the standing close mean? Control? Or just how she works? Honestly, I don't know yet. Four days isn't enough. I'll watch what she does for a month before I decide.
Omkar

qa.q: How long did Sunaina spend fixing the formulas with Omkar?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling in the morning when Sunaina stood close?
qa.a: Omkar felt tense and distrusted, shoulders up, reading her closeness as checking up; the evening's help hinted it might just be her way of working.

qa.q: Why is Omkar's plan to watch for a month wise?
qa.a: Four days of posture can mislead; what Sunaina does over time, like staying to help at six, will say more about her attitude than how she stands or sits.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see her own habit of standing beside the chair?
qa.a: She may see it as simply being hands-on and involved, not as control, which fits her staying late to fix the report.

grounding: Shows a young professional unsure how to read a boss's upright, close posture and choosing to judge by behaviour over time.

passage:
In her first week at the block development office in Tirupattur, Keerthana met two officers. The first, Mr. Selvam, leaned so far back in his chair during her briefing that it creaked, hands behind his head, eyes half closed. She walked out sure he thought her a waste of time.
The second, a woman officer from the district, sat bolt upright, stood very close at the file cabinet and fired quick questions. Keerthana felt she was being tested.
At lunch under the neem tree, Yamini, who had worked there six years, laughed. "Selvam sir leans back when he's relaxed with you. He does that only with people he likes. And Madam stands close with everyone; that's just how she talks."
Keerthana frowned. "So how am I supposed to know?"
"Watch what they do over a month. Who helps you. Who remembers what you said."

qa.q: Where did Keerthana and Yamini eat lunch?
qa.a: They ate lunch under the neem tree.

qa.q: What did Keerthana feel after the briefing with Mr. Selvam?
qa.a: Keerthana felt dismissed and discouraged, reading his leaned-back posture as boredom with her, though it might instead have been relaxed comfort.

qa.q: What does Yamini advise Keerthana to watch?
qa.a: What the officers do over a month: who helps her and who remembers what she said.

qa.q: Why might Yamini read Selvam's posture differently from Keerthana?
qa.a: Yamini has worked there six years and knows he leans back only with people he likes, while Keerthana had just one briefing to judge by.

grounding: Bosses' postures signal status and attitude differently from person to person, so behaviour over time says more than body position.
